statement: In people who smoked cigarettes and were motivated to quit (almost all adults), in 131 randomised and quasi-randomised trials (133 comparisons, 64,640 people; Cochrane review, search to July 2017), being offered nicotine replacement in any form (gum, patch, lozenge or tablet, inhaler, nasal or oral spray, a combination, or a choice of products), compared with a placebo product or no nicotine replacement and the same behavioural support in both groups, increased the number not smoking 6 months or more after the start of the quit attempt: about 6 more people in 100 (162 against 105 in 1,000; risk ratio 1.55, 95% CI 1.49 to 1.61; people lost to follow-up counted as smoking). In the review's table the gain is about 2 more in 100 where the trials gave limited behavioural support (62 against 40 in 1,000) and about 8 more in 100 where they gave intensive support (232 against 150 in 1,000); these baselines are the review's assumed rates, while the risk ratio is the observed pooled result. The risk ratio was similar for gum (1.49, 1.40 to 1.60; 56 comparisons), patch (1.64, 1.53 to 1.75; 51), lozenge or tablet (1.52, 1.32 to 1.74; 8), inhaler (1.90, 1.36 to 2.67; 4) and nasal spray (2.02, 1.49 to 2.73; 4), and higher for oral spray (2.48, 1.24 to 4.94) from one trial of 479 people; these are each product against its own placebo or no-product group, so they do not show which product is better (the head-to-head comparisons are in the claim on ways of using nicotine replacement compared directly). The result held when high-risk trials were left out (1.61, 1.52 to 1.69), in the 12 trials at low risk of bias in every respect (1.53, 1.37 to 1.71) and in placebo-controlled trials (1.61, 1.53 to 1.70), but not clearly in 4 trials in antenatal clinics (1.22, 0.92 to 1.62). Follow-up ran from 6 to 24 months. Two small trials in adolescents did not detect an effect, and the authors say there is little evidence for people who smoke fewer than about 10 to 15 cigarettes a day. They also say that unpublished trials with less favourable results may be missing (the funnel plot is somewhat asymmetric) and that the size of the effect may be smaller than estimated, though in their view not enough to change the results significantly. By the editors' count about three in five of the 136 included studies named a drug company as funder or supplier of study product, and the review did not analyse results by funder. Certainty: high. Status: replicated.
plain: People who wanted to stop smoking were more likely to have stopped 6 months or more later if they were given nicotine gum, patches, lozenges, sprays or inhalers than if they were given a dummy product or nothing: about 16 in 100 against about 10 or 11 in 100, so about 6 more in 100. The gain was about 2 more in 100 where people got little support and about 8 more in 100 where they got a lot. Each kind of product did better than its own comparison group. These were people trying to stop, so the trials do not show what nicotine replacement does for anyone else. Small trials with poor results may be missing, and drug companies paid for many of the trials, so the true gain could be somewhat smaller.
population: People who smoked cigarettes and were motivated to quit, almost all adults (two small trials in adolescents), in clinics, primary care, hospitals, antenatal clinics, community and over-the-counter-like settings; 131 randomised or quasi-randomised trials, 133 comparisons, 64,640 people; Cochrane review, search to July 2017
exposure: Being offered nicotine replacement in any form (gum, patch, lozenge or sublingual tablet, inhaler, nasal spray, oral spray, a combination or a choice of products)
comparator: A placebo product or no nicotine replacement, with the same behavioural support in both groups (the amount of support differed between trials)
outcome: Not smoking 6 months or more after the start of the quit attempt (strictest definition each trial reported, confirmed with a breath or body test in most trials, people lost to follow-up counted as smoking)
magnitude: Abstinence at 6+ months: RR 1.55 (95% CI 1.49–1.61), fixed-effect, I² 39%, 133 comparisons (131 trials), 64,640 participants; the review's table assumes 105 per 1,000 without NRT and gives 162 per 1,000 (156–168) with it (difference 57 per 1,000, about 6 in 100, editors' subtraction). Limited behavioural support 40 vs 62 per 1,000 (60–64; about 2 more in 100); intensive support 150 vs 232 per 1,000 (224–242; about 8 more in 100). By product (RR; comparisons; participants): gum 1.49 (1.40–1.60; 56; 22,581; I² 40%), patch 1.64 (1.53–1.75; 51; 25,754; I² 24%), lozenge or tablet 1.52 (1.32–1.74; 8; 4,439; I² 71%), inhaler 1.90 (1.36–2.67; 4; 976), nasal spray 2.02 (1.49–2.73; 4; 887), oral spray 2.48 (1.24–4.94; 1 trial; 479), choice of product 1.37 (1.25–1.52; 7; 8,288). Sensitivity: without high-risk trials 1.61 (1.52–1.69); the 12 low-risk trials 1.53 (1.37–1.71); biochemically validated trials 1.62 (1.55–1.70); placebo-controlled trials 1.61 (1.53–1.70). Antenatal clinics 1.22 (0.92–1.62; 4 trials; 1,675). Follow-up 6 to 24 months.

evidence.locator: Summary of findings, Table 1; Results › Effects of interventions › Any type of NRT versus placebo or no NRT control, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Any form of NRT against placebo or no NRT, abstinence at 6 months or longer (follow-up 6 to 24 months): RR 1.55 (95% CI 1.49 to 1.61), fixed-effect, I² 39%, 133 comparisons from 131 trials, 64,640 participants. The table assumes 105 per 1,000 without NRT and gives 162 per 1,000 (156 to 168) with NRT, a difference of 57 per 1,000 (editors' subtraction: about 6 in 100). The authors rate the evidence high certainty (GRADE).

evidence.locator: Summary of findings, Table 1 (limited and intensive behavioural support rows)
evidence.extracted: Limited behavioural support: 40 per 1,000 without NRT against 62 per 1,000 (60 to 64) with NRT; intensive behavioural support: 150 against 232 per 1,000 (224 to 242). Editors' subtraction: about 2 and about 8 more people in 100.

evidence.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Any type of NRT versus placebo or no NRT control, table after the 1st paragraph; Data and analyses, Comparison 1
evidence.extracted: RR by product (comparisons; participants): gum 1.49 (1.40 to 1.60; 56; 22,581; I² 40%); patch 1.64 (1.53 to 1.75; 51; 25,754; I² 24%); tablets or lozenges 1.52 (1.32 to 1.74; 8; 4,439; I² 71%); inhalator 1.90 (1.36 to 2.67; 4; 976); intranasal spray 2.02 (1.49 to 2.73; 4; 887); oral spray 2.48 (1.24 to 4.94; 1 trial; 479); choice of product 1.37 (1.25 to 1.52; 7; 8,288). Product estimates are subgroups of trials each against its own control group, not head-to-head comparisons.

evidence.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Any type of NRT versus placebo or no NRT control, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The I² of 71% in the lozenge or tablet subgroup is driven by one new trial (RR 1.08). Twelve trials had lower quit rates with NRT than control (every interval included no difference) and in a further 73% of trials the interval included no difference. One large patch trial in people with cardiovascular disease found 14% with the active patch against 11% with placebo quit at 6 months and 10% against 12% at 48 weeks.

evidence.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Sensitivity to risk of bias and study methods
evidence.extracted: Sensitivity analyses: excluding high-risk trials RR 1.61 (1.52 to 1.69); only the 12 low-risk trials 1.53 (1.37 to 1.71); excluding trials without biochemical validation 1.62 (1.55 to 1.70); placebo-controlled trials only 1.61 (1.53 to 1.70).

evidence.locator: Results › Risk of bias in included studies, 1st to 6th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: 12 trials low risk of bias in all domains and 36 high risk in at least one; adequate allocation concealment reported in 39 trials (29%); 43 trials had no matched placebo; 117 trials validated abstinence biochemically; follow-up was only 6 months in 15 gum, 19 patch, 4 combination and 1 lozenge trial.

evidence.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Sensitivity to treatment settings, 1st paragraph; Data and analyses, Comparison 4
evidence.extracted: By setting: antenatal clinics RR 1.22 (0.92 to 1.62; 4 trials; 1,675 participants), the only setting without a statistically significant effect; the other settings 1.39 (hospitals) to 1.70 (smoking clinics).

evidence.locator: Discussion › Trials in special populations, 1st paragraph; Authors' conclusions › Implications for practice, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Two small adolescent trials (Moolchan 2005; Scherphof 2014) did not detect an effect on quitting at 6 months or longer; the authors say there is little evidence on NRT in people smoking fewer than 10 to 15 cigarettes a day.

evidence.locator: Discussion › Limitations of the evidence base, 1st paragraph; Summary of findings, Table 1 footnotes 1 and 2
evidence.extracted: Authors: unpublished trials with less favourable results may be missing; the funnel plot shows some asymmetry; a cited meta-analysis (Etter 2007) found pharmaceutical-funded gum and patch trials had slightly higher effect sizes; the magnitude of effectiveness may be smaller than estimated. The table footnotes give the reasons for not downgrading: restricting to low-risk trials did not alter the effect, and with so many trials the asymmetry does not suggest that adding smaller trials with lower risk ratios would change the results significantly.
evidence.quote: the magnitude of the effectiveness of NRT may be smaller than our estimates suggest

evidence.locator: Characteristics of included studies › Notes of each study (editors' count)
evidence.extracted: Editors' count of the 136 included entries: about 80 name a drug company as funder, co-funder or supplier of study product, about 40 name only government, charity or university funders, about 15 report no source. The review did not analyse results by funder. Approximate: some entries are two halves of one trial and some company links are product supply only.

publication_bias.note: Funnel plot somewhat asymmetric; about three in five trials with drug-company links (editors' count); not rated down, following the authors' reasoning; a stricter reading would be one level.

grade.reasoning: Randomised evidence, starting high, read through a Cochrane review with a fixed-effect meta-analysis (AMSTAR 2: high confidence, on the study card); the review rates the main outcome high. Risk of bias, not rated down: most trials were at unclear or high risk of bias (12 of 136 low in every respect, 36 high in at least one, adequate allocation concealment in 39), but the result in the 12 low-risk trials (1.53), in placebo-controlled trials (1.61) and in trials with biochemical confirmation (1.62) is as large as the overall 1.55, so the weaker trials do not appear to be producing the effect. Inconsistency, not rated down: I² 39%; 12 trials had lower quit rates with nicotine replacement than with control, each with an interval that included no difference; the lozenge or tablet subgroup (I² 71%) is driven by one trial. Indirectness, not rated down because the claim is limited to people motivated to quit in trials, ranks no product and says nothing about people who use nicotine without trying to quit. Imprecision, not rated down: 64,640 people and an interval of 1.49 to 1.61. Publication bias, not rated down but recorded: the funnel plot is somewhat asymmetric, the authors say unpublished trials with less favourable results may be missing and that the size of the effect may be smaller than estimated, a study they cite found slightly larger effects in drug-company-funded trials, and by the editors' count about three in five included studies name a drug company as funder or supplier of study product (the review did not analyse by funder). The authors judge that, with so many trials, adding smaller trials with lower ratios would not change the results significantly, and the better-controlled subsets show effects at least as large; the editors follow that reasoning but record that a stricter reading, taking the asymmetry and the company links as probable inflation, would give moderate. The same standard is applied to the vape claims, where the equivalent argument (many trials) is not available. Status replicated: the result comes from many trials by many groups, 12 of which pointed the other way (none with an interval excluding no difference); earlier versions of the same review are not counted as replication.

verification.flag_note: The brief's single claim on nicotine replacement (cl_nic_nrt) is staged as three: this one (against placebo or no replacement, by form), cl_nic_nrt_forms (ways of using it compared head to head, from the 2023 review) and cl_nic_nrt_harms (side effects and serious events), because their certainty differs and one claim carries one rating. Certainty follows Cochrane's high rating; the editors' reservation (funnel asymmetry, company links in about three in five trials, the authors' own wording that the effect may be smaller) is in the grade reasoning, and a stricter reading would be moderate. The baseline rates in the review's table are assumed rates, so the absolute figures are illustrative; the risk ratio is the observed result. Not read: individual trial risk-of-bias tables, Appendix 3 beyond the text, forest and funnel figures (images), reference lists. Overlap of trials between this review and the 2023 review (Theodoulou) was not checked; the two claims answer different questions. Reference records exist (hartmann-boyce_2018); no new reference is needed.

statement: In adults who smoked cigarettes and stopped for more than 18 hours, in prospective studies that compared people's ratings after stopping with their own ratings before (15 core studies of 11 to 178 people, as summarized second-hand in a single-author narrative review that searched 1990 to 2004 and added earlier studies for symptoms left unclear before; Hughes, 2007), stopping is associated with more anger or irritability, anxiety, difficulty concentrating, impatience, restlessness and waking during the night, often with more vivid dreams; in most of these studies these symptoms peaked within the first week and were back at or near the pre-quit level within 2 to 4 weeks (1 week for restlessness in one study). Across all the studies reviewed, including earlier ones, low mood rose in most that measured it but not in all, drowsiness gave contradictory results, and fatigue, headaches, sweating, a racing heart, tremor and skin rash were not found to rise; constipation, cough and mouth ulcers rose in one study each, and dizziness in two, with other studies not finding them. The review gives no sizes or frequencies: it counts studies, and its author chose the results on his own judgment. The 2-to-4-week course is an average: in two studies 38% and 61% of people followed other courses, with symptoms rising again around the third week or not falling, and one later study suggests that recalling withdrawal makes it seem longer than it was. Craving, hunger and weight were outside the review. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: When people stop smoking, studies that asked them how they felt before and after found more irritability, anxiety, restlessness, trouble concentrating and waking at night. These were usually worst in the first week and mostly gone within 2 to 4 weeks, but in some people they lasted longer or came back. Tiredness, headaches and sweating did not go up. This comes from one expert's summary of older studies, which counted studies rather than measuring how strong the feelings were.
population: Adults who smoked cigarettes and stopped for more than 18 hours, in prospective studies: placebo or no-treatment arms of cessation trials, people quitting on their own, and people abstaining for a study
exposure: Stopping smoking cigarettes, followed from the first day to up to a year
comparator: The same people's ratings before stopping; a separate control group in 2 of the 15 core studies
outcome: Self-reported withdrawal symptoms (anger or irritability, anxiety, low mood, difficulty concentrating, drowsiness, fatigue, impatience, sleep problems, physical symptoms, restlessness) and how long they last
magnitude: No sizes, rates or intervals: counts of studies as summarized, for example anger lasting 2 weeks in 7 studies, 3 weeks in 1 and 4 weeks or more in 2; fatigue unchanged in 3 of 4 studies; sleep fragmentation increased in studies lasting 5 to 14 days; in two studies 38% and 61% of people did not follow the average course.

evidence.locator: Abstract; Method › Study selection and synthesis, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Data extraction and synthesis, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: A single-author review searching 1990 to 2004, with earlier studies also included for symptoms the 1990 review had left unclear: more than 3,500 citations, 792 abstracts read, 290 articles read and 120 cited; inclusion required published prospective studies of cigarettes with more than 18 hours of abstinence; the author chose which results to include on his subjective opinion of rigor, consistency and size, and states that data collection and interpretation rested solely on his judgments.

evidence.locator: Results › Description of abstinence effects, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Table 1
evidence.extracted: Conclusions rest mainly on 15 comprehensive prospective studies of 11 to 178 people: all but one had pre-quit values, 9 used control arms of trials, and only 2 had control groups, 2 generalizable samples, 3 more than 90 participants and 5 low attrition; no meta-analysis was done because of methodological heterogeneity.

evidence.locator: Results › Anger/irritability/frustration, 2nd paragraph; Anxiety, 2nd paragraph; Depression, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Anger peaks within the first week and lasts 2 weeks (7 studies), 3 weeks (1) or 4 weeks or more (2); anxiety rose in the first 1 to 3 days and lasted about 2 weeks in most studies, though one study of well-validated abstainers found a fall; low mood rose in 6 core studies but not in 2 (a third found a fall), peaking at 1, 2 or 3 weeks and still raised at 30 days in two, and the author calls this evidence surprisingly mixed.

evidence.locator: Results › Difficulty concentrating, 2nd paragraph (p. 319); Impatience, 2nd paragraph (p. 320); Insomnia (pp. 320-321); Restlessness, 2nd paragraph (p. 322)
evidence.extracted: Difficulty concentrating peaked in the first few days and lasted from a week or less to 4 weeks or more; impatience rose for 3 to 4 weeks or more in all 3 newer studies; sleep fragmentation (waking at night) increased consistently in sleep-EEG and clinical studies lasting 5 to 14 days, with more recall of vivid dreams; restlessness peaked on days 1 to 3 and lasted 2 to 4 weeks (1 week in one study).

evidence.locator: Results › Drowsiness/decreased alertness or arousal, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Fatigue (p. 320); Physical symptoms, 1st to 4th paragraphs (pp. 321-322)
evidence.extracted: Alertness fell in 2, rose in 2 and did not change in 3 core studies; fatigue did not change in 3 of 4 studies; all studies were negative for headaches, sweating, a racing heart, tremor and skin rash; dizziness rose transiently in two studies but not in a third; constipation, cough and mouth ulcers were each found in one study.

Total withdrawal scores were back at or very near pre-quit levels after about 2 weeks and by 3 to 4 weeks, so the author states that the syndrome lasts 2 to 4 weeks; onset could not be determined; in two studies 38% and 61% of people did not follow the average course (symptoms rose again about 3 weeks after quitting, or did not fall); one study suggests retrospective reports overestimate duration; prolonged withdrawal of 6 months or more does not appear to occur, except possibly for craving and hunger.

risk_of_bias.note: Almost all core studies compare ratings before and after quitting without a control group; outcomes are self-reported; the review did not appraise the studies and they cannot be appraised second-hand.

inconsistency.note: Consistent direction for the core symptoms; low mood and drowsiness are inconsistent and the claim says so.

indirectness.note: Seen only through a single-author narrative review that chose results on judgment (METHODS §6.3: second-hand).

imprecision.note: No estimate is claimed; the statement gives counts and says that sizes and frequencies are unknown.

publication_bias.note: Published studies only; not assessable here; not downgraded further.

grade.reasoning: Prospective within-person studies start low (METHODS §6.3). Risk of bias −1 (before-after comparisons without controls in almost all core studies, self-report, no appraisal) and indirectness −1 (seen only through a narrative review whose author chose the results) give very low. Status replicated: the core symptoms rose in studies by several independent groups (for example Gilbert et al., Jorenby et al., Ward et al. and West et al., besides the author's own), although 5 of the 15 core studies are his group's and low mood is mixed. The claim rests only on a narrative review, so it stays at draft and says its figures are second-hand.
